claims.text: Stainless steel has a native passive oxide layer.
The native passive oxide layer is less effective under extreme corrosive conditions.
Physical Vapor Deposition can deposit a thin, adherent film on stainless steel.
A PVD coating such as TiN can be made dense and uniform on stainless steel.
High chloride concentrations, acidic conditions, and high humidity at elevated temperatures are aggressive environments in which the native oxide layer may be insufficient.
The deposited coating is chemically inert and prevents penetration by corrosive species.
The PVD coating acts as a protective barrier that reduces contact between the corrosive environment and the stainless steel substrate.
Reduced contact with the corrosive environment hinders ion diffusion and localized corrosion processes.
Applying a dense, uniform PVD coating such as TiN improves the corrosion resistance of stainless steel in extreme environments.
PVD-coated stainless steel will have a lower corrosion rate than uncoated stainless steel under identical harsh conditions.
PVD-coated stainless steel will exhibit improved durability relative to uncoated stainless steel under harsh environmental conditions.
Uncoated stainless steel exhibits higher corrosion rates and more rapid degradation than PVD-coated stainless steel under identical conditions.
The corrosion-resistance improvement depends on coating adhesion, thickness, and stability.
The PVD coating material and deposition-process parameters influence corrosion performance.
The magnitude of the corrosion-resistance improvement may vary with the corrosive medium and operating conditions.
